scenarios.title: The dashboard cliff
scenarios.situation: Monday morning, the revenue dashboard shows a 60% drop starting Saturday. Slack is panicking. You own the pipeline that feeds the dashboard.
choices: Check pipeline health and data freshness first; a broken or stale feed explains a cliff better than a real business collapse
Announce the revenue drop to leadership immediately so they can react
Rebuild the dashboard from scratch; the visualization is probably misconfigured
Query production directly and overwrite the dashboard numbers
scenarios.why: Dashboards show data, not truth: a sudden cliff on a weekend boundary is the classic signature of a failed job, an expired credential, or a schema change upstream. Verifying freshness and run status takes minutes and prevents a false alarm from becoming a panicked business decision.
scenarios.hint: What changed at the exact moment the line drops: the business, or the data about the business?

scenarios.title: Pick the chart
scenarios.situation: You need to show the distribution of customer support response times: most replies land in 1-2 hours, a long tail stretches to 48 hours. Your manager suggests a pie chart.
scenarios.prompt: Which visualization is honest and useful?
choices: A histogram, because it shows the shape of the distribution including the long tail that a pie would hide
A pie chart, since the manager asked for one and stakeholders understand pies
A single big number showing the average response time
A 3D exploded pie chart to make the tail slice stand out
scenarios.why: Distributions need distributions: a histogram reveals skew, clusters, and outliers that define the real customer experience. A pie chart forces continuous data into a few arbitrary buckets, and a lone average hides the 48-hour tail entirely. The chart must serve the data, not the requester's comfort.
scenarios.hint: Which option still shows you the customers who waited two days?

scenarios.title: The multiplying join
scenarios.situation: You join orders to order_items on order_id and the row count triples. Revenue summed from the joined table is now 3x the finance report. The join keys look correct.
scenarios.prompt: What happened and how do you fix the metric?
evidence:
orders: 50,000 rows
order_items: 148,000 rows
joined: 148,000 rows (expected ~148k... but revenue x3?)
choices: The join fanned out: duplicate order_ids in orders multiplied item rows; deduplicate or aggregate to the right grain before joining, then re-sum
The database is corrupt; restore from backup
Finance's report is wrong; trust the joined query
Add DISTINCT to the SELECT and move on
scenarios.why: Joining tables at different grains multiplies rows when the 'one' side is not actually unique: each duplicated order row fans out across its items. DISTINCT masks the symptom without fixing the grain. The fix is to establish the correct grain (one row per order_item) and aggregate measures at that grain before or during the join.
scenarios.hint: If order_id were truly unique in orders, could the row count still triple?

scenarios.title: PII in the export
scenarios.situation: Marketing asks for 'all customer data' to build segments in a third-party tool. The export you would send includes names, emails, and full purchase history. There is no data-sharing agreement covering this tool.
choices: Refuse the raw export; offer an aggregated or de-identified dataset that answers their segmentation question without exposing PII to an unvetted tool
Send the full export; marketing needs data to do their job
Send it but delete the email addresses, keeping names for personalization
Upload it and let legal sort it out later if there is a problem
scenarios.why: Data minimization is the core governance principle: share the least data that answers the question. Names plus purchase history still identify people, and an unvetted third party with no agreement is an uncontrolled copy of customer PII. Aggregates or tokenized IDs give marketing their segments without creating a breach-sized exposure.
scenarios.hint: What is the smallest dataset that still answers their question?

scenarios.title: The schema changed overnight
scenarios.situation: Three downstream dashboards broke at 3 AM. The upstream team renamed 'user_id' to 'customer_id' and changed timestamps from UTC to local time, with no notice. This is the third silent breaking change this quarter.
scenarios.prompt: What systemic fix prevents the fourth?
choices: Establish a data contract: versioned schemas, advance notice of breaking changes, and CI checks that fail the upstream build if the contract breaks
Have your team check the upstream schema manually every morning
Copy the upstream table hourly so you always have the latest, whatever it looks like
Ask the upstream team nicely to be more careful
scenarios.why: Silent breaking changes are a coordination failure, not a technical one: downstream teams cannot defend against changes they cannot see. A data contract makes the schema a versioned API with the same discipline as code: breaking changes get a new version, notice, and automated checks. Manual checks and politeness do not scale.
scenarios.hint: How do software teams prevent exactly this class of surprise between services?

scenarios.title: Two definitions of active
scenarios.situation: Marketing reports 80,000 'active users'; product reports 45,000. Both queries run against the same warehouse. Marketing counts any login in 30 days; product counts completing a core action. The CEO wants one number for the board.
choices: Define one governed metric with a written definition, get stakeholder sign-off, implement it once in a shared semantic layer, and point every report at it
Average the two numbers and report 62,500
Pick whichever number is bigger; boards like growth
Let each team keep its number and add footnotes to the board deck
scenarios.why: Conflicting metrics are a definitions problem: two queries can both be 'correct' against different definitions. Averaging or footnoting preserves the confusion. The fix is governance: one written definition, one implementation, one source of truth, so every consumer of 'active users' means the same thing.
scenarios.hint: Is this a query bug or a language bug?

lessons.title: Data — Core concepts
concepts: Tidy data has one structure: each variable a column, each observation a row, each value a cell. Most 'messy data' pain is data that violates this shape.
Pipelines fail silently more often than loudly: build freshness checks, row-count assertions, and schema validation into every run, and alert on the checks, not just on crashes.
Grain is everything in analysis: know what one row represents before you join or aggregate, because joining at mixed grains multiplies rows and corrupts sums.
Visualize honestly: the chart type must match the data shape, axes must not deceive, and a single average never describes a distribution.
Governance is data's immune system: lineage (where it came from), minimization (least PII that answers the question), contracts (versioned schemas), and retention rules.
Raw data is irreplaceable: never overwrite source extracts; transformations should be re-runnable from immutable raw inputs.

example.code:
$ sqlite3 orders.db "SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows, COUNT(customer_id) AS non_null FROM orders;"
152340|152301
example.walkthrough: A thirty-second profile: total rows versus non-null keys. The 39 null customer_ids are joins that will silently drop or fan out downstream; find them now, not in the board deck.

pitfalls: Common trap: joining on keys you never checked for uniqueness, then reporting multiplied metrics.
Common trap: truncated y-axes and cherry-picked date ranges that manufacture trends.
Common trap: overwriting raw extracts with cleaned data, destroying the ability to re-derive or audit.
Common trap: emailing PII exports to answer questions that aggregates could answer.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Profile a messy CSV
labs.objective: Import a messy CSV into sqlite and quantify its data-quality problems.
steps: Import customers.csv into a sqlite table with .import.
Count total rows, null emails, and duplicate customer_ids.
Find the min and max of signup_date and flag any future dates.
List the top 5 most common malformed phone values.
Write the findings and recommended cleaning rules to profile.txt.

checks.hint: Your profiling queries should return pipe-separated counts.
The profile must quantify duplicates, nulls, and bad dates.

labs.title: Build a repeatable pipeline script
labs.objective: Write a shell pipeline that extracts, validates, and loads data with checksums so reruns are safe.
steps: Write pipeline.sh: download (or copy) the source file to raw/ with a date stamp.
Checksum the raw file with sha256sum and store the hash.
Validate: row count above minimum, required columns present, no future dates.
Abort with a clear error if any check fails; load to sqlite only on success.
Run it twice and confirm the second run is idempotent.

checks.hint: Verify the raw file checksum is recorded before any transformation.
The script should print OK only when all validations pass.

simulations.title: The dirty CSV
simulations.brief: The nightly pipeline failed at 2 AM. The error says 'malformed row 48,211.' The dashboard the CEO checks at 8 AM is now stale. Fix the pipeline without corrupting the data.

steps.symptom: Pipeline failed on row 48,211 of the customer export. The file came from a vendor.
evidence:
Row 48,211: expected 12 columns, found 14
Source: vendor export customers_2026-10-07.csv
Downstream: CEO dashboard (stale since 02:00)
options: Delete row 48,211 and re-run
Inspect the row first: quoted commas or embedded newlines are the usual cause — then fix the parser, not the data
Re-run the pipeline and hope it was transient
Ask the vendor for a new file and wait
steps.explain: Malformed rows are usually a parsing problem, not a data problem: quoted fields containing commas, or embedded newlines splitting one row into two. Deleting the row destroys evidence (and maybe a real customer); fixing the parser fixes every future file too.

steps.symptom: Confirmed: the vendor wraps addresses in quotes, and some contain commas. The parser was splitting on every comma.
evidence:
48210,"Acme, Inc.",...  <- quoted comma
Parser: naive split(",") -> 14 columns instead of 12
options: Switch to a proper CSV parser that respects quoting, add a schema check (12 columns), and quarantine bad rows instead of failing the whole run
Tell the vendor to stop using commas in addresses
Keep the naive split but skip quoted rows
Process the file by hand in a spreadsheet
steps.explain: Real CSV parsing respects quoting — that is what the format is for. And pipelines should degrade gracefully: schema-check every row, quarantine the bad ones for review, and let the good 48,210 flow. One bad row should never hold a dashboard hostage.

steps.symptom: Pipeline is green. The CEO asks why the dashboard was stale this morning.
evidence: CEO: 'The numbers were frozen at 2 AM. What happened?'
options: 'The vendor sent us a bad file.'
'A malformed vendor row failed the load; we fixed the parser, quarantined the bad rows for review, and added alerting so the next failure pages us instead of greeting you at 8 AM.'
'These things happen with data.'
Blame the vendor by name in the all-hands
steps.explain: Data incidents get the same honest treatment as outages: what broke, what you changed, and what prevents recurrence. 'The vendor sent a bad file' is true but useless — the fix is yours to own.

simulations.debrief: You diagnosed the parser instead of blaming the data, built graceful degradation into the pipeline, and reported honestly. Messy data is the job — pipelines that survive it are the skill.

simulations.title: Correlation is not causation
simulations.brief: Marketing found it: ice-cream sales and signup spikes move together (r=0.91). They want the all-hands slide to say 'ice cream drives signups.' You own the data. Decide what the chart can honestly say.

steps.symptom: The correlation is real: r=0.91 over 12 months. Marketing wants a causal claim for the campaign.
evidence:
ice_cream_sales vs signups, monthly, n=12
Pearson r = 0.91, p < 0.01
Marketing draft: 'Ice cream drives signups — summer campaign approved'
options: Approve the causal claim — the numbers back it
Block the causal claim: check for a confounder first (season is the obvious one), and report only what the data supports
Ask for a bigger sample before deciding
Let marketing say whatever sells
steps.explain: A strong correlation with an obvious confounder — summer drives both — is the textbook trap. The honest move is to test the confounder (seasonality) before anyone prints a causal claim. r=0.91 tells you they move together; it says nothing about why.

steps.symptom: Seasonality confirmed: both series peak in summer, flat otherwise. Within-season correlation is 0.12.
evidence:
Within-month correlation: r = 0.12 (noise)
Driver: summer season -> more outings -> both rise
options: Publish the 0.91 anyway — it is technically accurate
Report the honest finding: 'No meaningful relationship after accounting for season. Do not base the campaign on this.'
Bury the analysis so marketing is not embarrassed
Find a different variable that correlates and pitch that
steps.explain: Technically-accurate-but-misleading is still misleading. Your job is the honest finding, delivered plainly, with the evidence attached. Killing a bad campaign with data is one of the highest-value things an analyst does.

steps.symptom: Marketing is disappointed. They ask what analysis WOULD support a campaign decision.
evidence: Marketing: 'Fine — what should we measure instead?'
options: 'Nothing — data cannot help marketing.'
Propose a real test: run the campaign in half the regions (randomized), compare signup lift against control, and pre-register the success metric before launch
Suggest a bigger correlational study
Tell them to trust their gut
steps.explain: Do not just kill the bad analysis — replace it with a good one. A randomized regional rollout with a pre-registered metric turns 'does it work?' from an argument into an experiment. That is the analyst's real product: better questions, answered honestly.

simulations.debrief: You caught the confounder, refused to launder correlation into causation, and replaced the bad analysis with an experiment. Data literacy is mostly the discipline to say 'not proven' when everyone wants a story.

simulations.title: PII in the warehouse
simulations.brief: Routine audit, routine horror: the analytics warehouse has unmasked emails and phone numbers in three tables that 40 analysts can query. Respond — carefully, because the data is already everywhere.

steps.symptom: Three warehouse tables contain plaintext PII. Forty analysts have query access. The tables feed six dashboards.
evidence:
Tables: users_raw, events_raw, support_tickets
PII: email + phone, unmasked | access: 40 analysts
Downstream: 6 dashboards, 2 vendor exports
options: Delete the tables immediately
Contain first: revoke broad access to a need-to-know group, mask the columns, then trace every downstream copy before deciding on deletion
Email all 40 analysts asking them to delete any exports
Do nothing — the data was collected legitimately
steps.explain: You cannot un-spread data, so you sequence it: stop the spread (narrow access, mask columns), map where it already went (dashboards, exports), then remediate. Immediate deletion destroys the evidence of exposure and breaks six dashboards with no plan.

steps.symptom: Contained. Now: who accessed the PII, and was any of it exfiltrated?
evidence:
90 days of query history available
2 vendor exports included the PII columns
1 analyst downloaded 2M rows last month (says it was for a churn model)
options: Assume the downloads were innocent
Review the query logs against business justification, interview the analyst, notify legal/compliance, and follow the incident process
Fire the analyst who downloaded the rows
Delete the query logs to limit liability
steps.explain: PII exposure is a governance incident, not just a technical one: legal and compliance own the notification decisions, and the query logs are evidence — you preserve them, not purge them. The analyst gets a fair review, not a summary judgment.

steps.symptom: Incident closed. Build the system that prevents the next one.
evidence: PII never lands unmasked in the warehouse again
options: Ban analysts from querying raw tables
Classify data at ingestion, mask PII by default with an approval flow for unmasking, and add automated PII detection to the pipeline
Trust the team to be careful now
Move the warehouse on-premises
steps.explain: Governance that works is built into the pipeline: classification at ingestion, masking by default, unmasking by approval, and automated detection as the backstop. 'Be careful' is not a control; a masked-by-default warehouse is.

simulations.debrief: You contained before purging, treated exposure as a governance incident with evidence preserved, and built masking into the pipeline. Data governance is not paperwork — it is architecture.

simulations.title: The metric that moved
simulations.brief: Activation rate dropped 12 points overnight. Product wants to roll back yesterday's release. But the release touched nothing near activation. Find out what actually moved.

steps.symptom: Activation: 64% -> 52% overnight. Yesterday's release changed the billing page only.
evidence:
Activation rate: 64% -> 52% (overnight)
Yesterday's release: billing page copy changes only
Product: 'Roll it back now.'
options: Roll back the billing release immediately
Check the metric definition and pipeline first — a 12-point overnight move with no plausible cause smells like a measurement change, not a product change
Blame seasonality
Wait a week to see if it recovers
steps.explain: When the cause cannot plausibly produce the effect, suspect the measurement. Metric definitions, pipeline filters, and event instrumentation change silently — and a broken funnel definition moves the number without moving reality.

steps.symptom: Found it: the analytics SDK update last night renamed the 'activated' event. The funnel counts the old name. Real activations are flat.
evidence:
SDK 4.2 renamed event 'activated' -> 'activation_completed'
Funnel definition: still counts 'activated' (old name)
True activations: flat at 64%
options: Fix the funnel to count both event names, backfill, and add an event-schema contract test to CI
Rename the event back in the SDK
Tell product the metric was wrong and move on
Freeze all SDK updates
steps.explain: Fix the definition (count both names during transition), backfill the history so trends stay true, and add a contract test so the next rename breaks CI instead of the dashboard. Metrics are code — they get tests like code.

steps.symptom: Metric restored. Product still wants someone to blame for the scare.
evidence: Product: 'Whose fault was the bad number?'
options: Blame the SDK team
'Nobody's — and that's the point. The system allowed a silent metric break. We fixed the definition, backfilled, and added contract tests. The scare is now impossible to repeat.'
Blame the analyst who built the funnel
Promise it will never happen again
steps.explain: Metric incidents get the blameless treatment too: the failure was systemic (no contract between SDK and funnel), and the fix is systemic. 'Never happen again' is a promise you cannot keep; 'cannot happen silently again' is one you can.

simulations.debrief: You suspected the measurement before the product, fixed the definition with backfill, and turned a scare into contract tests. When a metric moves impossibly, check the ruler before the thing being measured.

simulations.title: To publish or not
simulations.brief: The research team wants to publish an 'anonymized' dataset of user behavior. You can see the quasi-identifiers from here. Decide whether it ships.

steps.symptom: The dataset is 'anonymized': names removed, but zip code, birth date, and gender remain. 50,000 rows.
evidence:
Rows: 50,000 | removed: names, emails
Kept: zip code, birth date, gender, behavior events
Claim: 'anonymized'
options: Approve — names are gone, so it is anonymous
Reject as-is: zip + birth date + gender uniquely identifies most Americans (the classic re-identification result). Require k-anonymity or aggregation first
Approve but add a terms-of-service banning re-identification
Publish only the summary statistics
steps.explain: Removing names is not anonymization — it is pseudonymization theater. The famous result stands: a handful of quasi-identifiers re-identify most people. A ToS ban on re-identification is a legal fig leaf, not a technical protection.

steps.symptom: The researchers push back: 'We need row-level data for the analysis. Aggregation kills the research.'
options: Cave and publish the rows
Offer the middle path: a governed research enclave (query access, no downloads, audited) or differential-privacy release with a stated epsilon budget
Tell them to find another dataset
Publish and hope nobody re-identifies
steps.explain: The honest negotiation: row-level utility without row-level exposure. A governed enclave or differential privacy gives researchers real analytical power with real privacy math. 'Publish and hope' is not a governance position.

steps.symptom: A release path is agreed. What do you document?
evidence: Document the release decision for the audit trail
options: Nothing — the decision is made
Document the privacy review: the re-identification risk found, the mitigation chosen, the epsilon budget or enclave controls, and the approval signatures
Write 'approved by data team'
Delete the original dataset to be safe
steps.explain: Privacy decisions are auditable decisions: what risk you found, what mitigation you chose, who approved it. If a regulator or a researcher asks in two years, the doc — not your memory — is the answer.

simulations.debrief: You recognized quasi-identifiers for what they are, negotiated a real privacy-preserving path, and documented the decision. Data ethics is not saying no — it is finding the yes that does not harm people.

consoleSims.title: Model the signups table
consoleSims.brief: The analytics project needs a signups table. Create it with an id, email, and created_at — then index the email column, because every lookup will filter on it.

tasks.instruction: Create a table named signups with columns: id INTEGER, email TEXT, created_at TEXT.

params.name: signups
params.columns: id INTEGER, email TEXT, created_at TEXT

tasks.hint: Create table: NAME=signups, COLUMNS='id INTEGER, email TEXT, created_at TEXT'.

tasks.instruction: Create an index on the email column of signups.
tasks.hint: Create index: TABLE=signups, COLUMN=email — index what you filter on.

consoleSims.debrief: Schema first, indexes on the access patterns. A table modeled around its queries stays fast as it grows.

consoleSims.title: Count what matters
consoleSims.brief: The stakeholder asks 'how many signups this week?' Write a query that counts rows in the signups table — the console validates that your SQL actually performs a COUNT.

tasks.instruction: Run a SQL query that counts the rows in signups (use COUNT).
tasks.hint: Type a query containing COUNT, e.g. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM signups — the console checks your SQL contains COUNT.

consoleSims.debrief: Every metric is a query. Writing the COUNT yourself — instead of trusting a dashboard — is how you know what the number actually means.

consoleSims.title: Provision the analytics database
consoleSims.brief: The analytics team needs its own database with least-privilege access. Create the analytics database, add a read-only user analyst_ro, and grant them SELECT only.

tasks.instruction: Grant SELECT on analytics to analyst_ro.
tasks.hint: Grant privilege: DB=analytics, USER=analyst_ro, PRIV=SELECT — read-only, nothing more.

consoleSims.debrief: Databases get owners, users get least privilege. analyst_ro can read and analyze — and cannot accidentally drop anything.

consoleSims.title: Back up before the migration
consoleSims.brief: The warehouse migration starts tomorrow. Create the analytics database in this console, then take a backup — migrations without backups are just hope with extra steps.

tasks.hint: Run a backup on the analytics database.

consoleSims.debrief: Backup before migration, always. The restore you never test is the restore that fails when you need it.

terminalMissions.title: Who is the analyst
terminalMissions.brief: Analyses are attributed. Print your username.
terminalMissions.success_message: Analyst identified. Every number has an author.

terminalMissions.title: Name the warehouse host
terminalMissions.brief: Data lives somewhere. Print the hostname of this machine.
terminalMissions.success_message: Host named. Lineage starts with location.

terminalMissions.title: List the datasets
terminalMissions.brief: Profile before you analyze: list what data is available here.

checks.hint: Run: ls — what datasets are here?

terminalMissions.success_message: Datasets listed. Never analyze data you have not inventoried.

terminalMissions.title: State the sample size
terminalMissions.brief: The dataset holds 6 records. State the sample size with echo — conclusions scale with n, so n gets stated.

checks.hint: Run: echo with the sample size (e.g. echo "n=6 records").

terminalMissions.success_message: Sample size stated. A number without its n is a rumor.

terminalMissions.title: Confirm the working directory
terminalMissions.brief: Reproducibility starts with context. Print your working directory.
terminalMissions.success_message: Context recorded. Reproducible work states where it ran.

terminalMissions.title: Check the platform
terminalMissions.brief: Print the full system information — the platform is part of the methodology section.
terminalMissions.success_message: Platform recorded. Methods sections include the machine.

terminalMissions.title: Publish the finding
terminalMissions.brief: State your headline finding with echo (the error rate is 33%), then print your identity record to sign the analysis.

checks.hint: Run: echo with the finding (e.g. echo "error rate 33 percent").

terminalMissions.success_message: Finding published and signed. Honest numbers, named author.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel
Funding: $190M Series F, July 2026 (Elephant-led); ~730 employees
Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.alt: A policy engine at the center of a small graph evaluates an access request from a finance user on an untrusted laptop to an R and D code server. The request is denied because there is no prior relationship edge and the device is untrusted.
media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.
media.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
media.caption: UEBA learns each user's normal hours, locations, and volumes, then scores deviations from that baseline.
media.alt: 24-hour timeline showing a shaded normal login window from 8 AM to 6 PM with normal logins inside it, and a red anomaly marker at 2:47 AM for a foreign login scoring 97 out of 100.

media.title: Indirect prompt injection attack flow
media.caption: An attacker hides instructions in data the agent retrieves; the agent mistakes data for instructions and misuses its tools.
media.alt: Attack flow diagram: hidden instruction in an email is read by an AI agent, which mistakes it for a command and calls a privileged tool, causing fraud; three defense boxes below: sanitize content, least-privilege tools, human approval.
